records.title: Saci-Pererê the One-Legged Trickster
records.summary: One of the most famous icons of Brazilian folklore, Saci-Pererê is a mischievous one-legged youth of indigenous Tupi-Guarani and Afro-Brazilian origin who wears a bright red magic cap (carapuça) and smokes a clay pipe. Saci travels inside localized wind whirlwinds (redemoinhos), blowing out campfire embers, souring boiling milk, braiding horses' manes into knots, and confusing forest travelers. Anyone who hurls a rosary or sieve into the center of a whirlwind can trap Saci and snatch his red cap, compelling the sprite to grant three wishes in exchange for its freedom.
records.historical_period: 18th Century Colonial Syncretism (popularized 1918 by Monteiro Lobato in O Sacy)
records.region_or_community: Southeast and Central-West Brazil, rural fazenda communities

records.title: Curupira the Backward-Footed Forest Guardian
records.summary: First documented in 1560 by Jesuit priest José de Anchieta, the Curupira is an ancient indigenous guardian spirit of the Brazilian Amazon and Atlantic rainforests. Manifesting as a short, flame-haired forest boy, his feet are uniquely turned backward, so that his footprints point in the opposite direction of his travel, hopelessly disorienting pursuers. Armed with uncanny whistles that mimic jungle birds, Curupira severely punishes hunters who slaughter nursing animals, fell sacred trees, or harvest more game than needed for sustenance, driving greedy poachers to madness.
alternate_names: The Backward-Footed Demon of the Woods
records.historical_period: Pre-Columbian Tupi Lore (first written record May 30, 1560 by José de Anchieta)
records.region_or_community: Amazon Basin and Atlantic Rainforest (Mata Atlântica)

records.title: Iara: The River Mermaid of the Amazon
records.summary: In Tupi indigenous mythology, Iara (from 'Uiara', meaning Lady of the Waters) was once a courageous indigenous warrior maiden so praised by her father that her jealous brothers plotted to murder her in the jungle. Defending herself, she killed them and fled, but was thrown into the confluence of the Negro and Solimões rivers by her father. The river fish took pity on her and transformed her into an enchanting water siren with radiant green eyes, long copper hair, and the tail of an aquatic serpent. Singing irresistible melodies from riverbanks at sunset, she lures fishermen and canoeists beneath the waves to her sunken crystal kingdom.
records.historical_period: Pre-Columbian Tupi lore, syncretized during colonial Amazonian navigation
records.region_or_community: Amazon River basin, Pará and Amazonas states

records.title: Boitatá: The Fiery Serpent of the Wetlands
records.summary: Recorded in Jesuit chronicles as early as 1560, Boitatá (from Tupi 'mboi tatá', meaning fiery serpent) is a giant serpent of pure luminescent fire that slithers through riverbanks, wetlands, and flooded savannas. According to legend, during a great catastrophic deluge of primordial night, the serpent survived by consuming the eyes of dead animals, absorbing their captured sunlight until its own body glowed with blinding flame. Boitatá acts as a fierce protector of virgin forests against arsonists and slash-and-burn hunters; anyone who gazes into its burning eyes is struck blind or driven mad, surviving only by remaining motionless with closed eyes.
alternate_names: The Fire Serpent of the Pantanal
records.historical_period: Pre-Columbian Tupi Lore (documented 1560 by José de Anchieta)
records.region_or_community: Pantanal wetlands, Mato Grosso and Amazon floodplains

records.title: The Pink River Dolphin (Boto Cor-de-Rosa)
records.summary: Dwelling in the dark, warm waters of the Amazon and Araguaia river systems, the pink river dolphin (Inia geoffrensis) is the protagonist of Brazil's definitive river shapeshifting legend. According to riverside folklore, on festive June festival nights (Festas Juninas), the pink boto transforms into a handsome, elegant gentleman dressed entirely in a crisp white linen suit and a white fedora hat to conceal the blowhole on top of his crown. Entering riverside village dances, the stranger charms the most beautiful young woman, seduces her, and impregnates her before diving back into the river at dawn to resume his aquatic dolphin form.
records.historical_period: Colonial Era to Living Amazonian Oral Tradition
records.region_or_community: Amazonas, Pará, and riverside river settlements

records.title: Mula Sem Cabeça: The Headless Mule
records.summary: A terrifying staple of Brazilian rural folklore, the Mula Sem Cabeça (Headless Mule) is the cursed manifestation of any woman who engages in romantic or physical intimacy with a Catholic priest. On Thursday nights at midnight, the woman transforms into a galloping phantom mule with silver horseshoes and flames shooting from her severed neck instead of a head. Galloping furiously past churches and across rural crossroads, her whinnying shrieks terrify horses and dogs. The curse can only be lifted if a brave traveler draws blood from the mule with a virgin iron blade or removes her iron halter.
records.historical_period: Colonial Portuguese Catholic Syncretism (17th Century to present)
records.region_or_community: Interior of São Paulo, Minas Gerais, and Goiás
geographic_associations: Interior crossroads of Minas Gerais and São Paulo

records.title: Caipora: The Guardian of Forest Game
records.summary: Closely related to Curupira, Caipora (from Tupi 'caapora', meaning forest dweller) is an indigenous forest deity depicted as a dark, hirsute youth or wild man riding an immense collared peccary (wild boar) and smoking an aromatic pipe. As the sovereign master of all forest animals, Caipora demands respect from hunters: if a hunter leaves tobacco on a tree stump before entering the brush, Caipora grants safe passage and one animal for dinner. If a hunter kills greedily on holy days or shoots a pregnant animal, Caipora drives the dogs wild, disorients the poacher in thorny thickets, and beats him with tree branches.
records.historical_period: Pre-Columbian Tupi Lore to Contemporary Sertão Folklore

records.title: The Mapinguari: Giant Amazonian Beast
records.summary: Feared by indigenous Karitiana and Machiguenga tribes across the southwestern Amazon Basin, the Mapinguari is a towering, nine-foot-tall bipedal beast covered in reddish-brown matted fur. Described as possessing a second gaping mouth on its belly and claws capable of shearing through jungle vines, the creature emits a sickening, rotten musk odor that immobilizes hunters. Modern biologists and folklorists theorize the legend preserves ancestral oral memories of the extinct giant ground sloth (Megatherium) that survived in deep Amazonian refuges alongside early indigenous human populations.
alternate_names: The Giant Ground Sloth of Acre
records.historical_period: Ancient Indigenous Oral Tradition to Contemporary Cryptozoology

records.title: Negrinho do Pastoreio: The Little Black Shepherd
records.summary: Deeply revered in the gaucho folklore of Rio Grande do Sul, Negrinho was an enslaved Afro-Brazilian orphan boy who tended horses for an exceptionally cruel rancher. When the rancher lost a horse race, he blamed the boy for losing a prize bay stallion, flogged him severely, and left him bound overnight atop an anthill to be devoured. The next morning, the rancher discovered the boy standing miraculously unharmed and glowing with divine light beside the Virgin Mary, with the lost stallion standing gently at his side. Today, gauchos across southern Brazil light a candle to Negrinho whenever they lose a cherished possession, knowing he unfailingly recovers lost items.
alternate_names: The Little Shepherd of the Pampas
records.historical_period: 19th Century Southern Brazil (popularized 1906 by Simões Lopes Neto)
records.region_or_community: Rio Grande do Sul, Southern Pampas

records.title: Cobra Grande: The Giant River Serpent of Pará
records.summary: Cobra Grande, or Boiúna, is a colossal black serpent that inhabits the profoundest abyssal trenches of the Amazon River in Pará. Born to an indigenous human mother, the serpent grew so enormous that she had to release it into the river. Swimming through the water, its massive body carves out river channels, while its glowing eyes appear as the navigational spotlights of a ghost steamboat at night. According to Belém urban folklore, the head of the sleeping Cobra Grande rests beneath the high altar of the Basilica of Our Lady of Nazareth, while its tail extends beneath the Guajará Bay; should the serpent ever awaken, the entire city of Belém will sink into the watery depths.
records.historical_period: Pre-Columbian Tupi myth to Colonial City Folklore of Belém
records.region_or_community: Belém, Pará and the Lower Amazon River
